zh.q: 桌上是些什么？教材图 12.3-1 这条电路是怎么接的？
zh.concl: 电压表接在「电池 + 开关」两端、电流表串在「变阻器」这条支路里（教材图 12.3-1）；变阻器按限流用，只接一端 + 滑片两个柱。开关断开时电压表读 0.00 V，不是读 E——E 要从 U-I 直线的截距外推。
points: 电压表跨的是「电池 + 开关」，开关落在它的跨接范围内——这就是图 12.3-1 的接法。
电流表串在「电流表 + 变阻器」这条支路里，变阻器按限流用（只用一端 + 滑片两个柱）。
开关断开时电压表读 0.00 V，不是读 E（常考）。

zh.q: 教材为什么先接线、把阻值调到较大，最后才闭合开关？
zh.concl: 教材的操作顺序：先按图接线、把阻值调到较大，再闭合开关、逐渐减小（p.91）；理由是「绝对不允许将电源两端用导线直接连接在一起」（p.87）——R 小到 0 时短路电流 2.50 A，表会顶格、电源会发烫。
points: 顺序是考点：先接线 → 滑片到最大 → 合开关 → 逐渐减小。
R 越小 I 越大、U 越小，两个读数必须同时读。
R 不能到 0：短路电流 2.50 A 是量程的 4 倍，p.87 明令禁止短接。

zh.q: 为什么不能只读一组？滑片从大往小减下去，两个表怎么变？
zh.concl: 只测两组「看起来比较简单，误差却可能较大；只有多次测量，并对数据进行处理，才能减小误差」（p.89）——所以用滑动变阻器改变外电阻、多测几组。U 随 I 增大而减小，是因为内阻上的电势降落 Ir 变大（p.86）。
points: 5 组要从大到小改变阻值，让 I 的跨度尽量大（0.07 → 0.58 A）。
记的是表上的读数（U、I），不是用 E、r 算出来的数。
I 越大 U 越小，因为内阻上的 Ir 变大。

zh.q: 把这 5 个点画到 U-I 图上，能得到什么？
zh.concl: 把式 (1) 改写成 U = −Ir + E（教材式 2）：纵截距 = 断路时的路端电压 = E，斜率绝对值 = r；U = 0 的交点给短路电流，r = E/I短 走第二条路，两条路给同一个 r。
points: 纵轴是 U、横轴是 I，直线的斜率是负的。
纵截距 = 断路时的路端电压 = E；斜率绝对值 = r。
U = 0 的交点是短路电流，r = E/I短 给同一个 r。

zh.q: 纵轴从 0 起，图变成什么样？截距变了吗？
zh.concl: 干电池内阻小、U 变化小，所以作图时「电压轴的起点坐标一般不从 0 开始」，应根据数据选起点（p.91）；只换坐标范围不改直线，所以 p.90 问「交点是否发生改变」——不改变（p.90 只问不答，按方程推出），截距仍是 E。
points: 干电池内阻小、U 变化小，纵轴起点一般不从 0 起。
起点只改坐标范围，直线和截距都不变。
数据挤在一小团时，要会说「调坐标轴范围」，而不是「数据不行」。

zh.q: 只记前两组、用两点联立解方程，会差多少？
zh.concl: 两点联立在数学上成立，但读数只到 0.01、两组之间 I 只差 0.03 A，ΔU 只有 2 个末位，除下去误差被放大——教材因此要求多次测量；取点跨度越大，两点法越接近五点法。
points: 两点法数学上对，但读数只有 0.01，ΔU 只有 2 个末位。
前两组 I 只差 0.03 A → r 偏到 0.67 Ω（+0.06 Ω）。
取首末两组（I 差 0.51 A）→ 回到 0.61 Ω：跨度才是关键。

zh.q: 把电流表串到电源那一支、电压表只跨变阻器，测出来的 r 还一样吗？
zh.concl: 接法一换，E 测出来还是 1.50 V，r 从 0.59 / 0.61 抬到 0.69 Ω（+0.09 Ω，+15 %，9 个末位）——电压表少读了电流表上的分压 I·R_A，这份少掉的电压被全算到斜率上，r 偏大、偏大量正好是电流表内阻（教材本节未讨论，属 L3 解析式推导）。
points: 接法决定系统误差的方向，不是「读数不同而已」。
对照接法：E 不偏、r 偏大 +R_A（读数级 +0.09 Ω，9 个末位，一测就看得出）。
这一档主读数测的是变阻器两端电压，不是路端电压——读数名字要跟着换。

zh.q: 教材那种接法会把 E、r 测偏大还是偏小？为什么读数里看不出来？
zh.concl: 教材接法的偏差是 E测、r测 都偏小、同比例；偏差比 0.01 的读数末位小 33 / 83 倍，2 位读数里根本看不出来——所以教材正文不讨论它，把力气花在多测、作图、纵轴起点上。方向只能靠解析式算，不能靠读数看出来（解析式推导，教材本节未讨论，L3）。
points: 电表不是理想表：R_V 分流、R_A 分压（p.76 给了约为 3 kΩ / 0.1 Ω）。
教材接法的偏差是 E测、r测 同比例偏小 0.0200 %（k = R_V/(R_V+r)）。
这个偏差比读数末位小 33 / 83 倍，读数上看不出来——方向只能算。

zh.q: 桌上这套接法，用它测出来的 E、r 能过关吗？
zh.concl: 判据只看结果：同工况 5 组、E测 与 1.50 V 差 ≤ 0.01 V、r测 与 0.60 Ω 差 ≤ 0.02 Ω。接法本身不是判据，但它决定结果——对照接法把电流表内阻算进了 r（0.69 Ω），教材接法的偏差只有 0.0200 %、读数看不出。
points: 判据只有三条：同工况 5 组、E测 与 1.50 V 差 ≤ 0.01 V、r测 与 0.60 Ω 差 ≤ 0.02 Ω。
进入时接法在对照接法：照它记 5 组得 0.69 Ω，差 0.09 → 必须自己想到换回教材接法。
记不满 5 组也过不了：组数也是「测出来」的一部分。

en.q: What's on the bench? How is the circuit in textbook Fig. 12.3-1 wired?
en.concl: The voltmeter is across "cell + switch" and the ammeter is in series in the "rheostat" branch (textbook Fig. 12.3-1); the rheostat is used as a current limiter, connecting just one end and the slider. With the switch open the voltmeter reads 0.00 V, not E; E has to be extrapolated from the intercept of the U-I line.
points: The voltmeter spans "cell + switch", so the switch is inside its span; that's the Fig. 12.3-1 circuit.
The ammeter is in series in the "ammeter + rheostat" branch, and the rheostat is a current limiter (only one end and the slider are used).
With the switch open the voltmeter reads 0.00 V, not E (commonly tested).

en.q: Why does the textbook wire up first, set the resistance high, and only then close the switch?
en.concl: The textbook's order: wire up per the diagram and set the resistance high, then close the switch and gradually reduce it (p.91); the reason is "never connect the two terminals of a source directly with a wire" (p.87). With R down to 0 the short-circuit current is 2.50 A, pinning the meter and heating the source.
points: The order is tested: wire up → slider to maximum → close switch → gradually reduce.
The smaller R, the larger I and the smaller U; read both meters at the same time.
R can't go to 0: the 2.50 A short-circuit current is 4 times the range, and p.87 forbids shorting.

en.q: Why not just read one set? As the slider goes from large to small, how do the two meters change?
en.concl: Measuring only two sets "looks simpler, but the error can be large; only repeated measurement with data processing reduces error" (p.89), so use the rheostat to change the external resistance and measure several sets. U falls as I rises because the potential drop Ir across the internal resistance grows (p.86).
points: Change the resistance from large to small over the 5 sets to make the range of I as wide as possible (0.07 → 0.58 A).
Record the meter readings (U, I), not numbers calculated from E and r.
The larger I, the smaller U, because Ir across the internal resistance grows.

en.q: Plot these 5 points on a U-I graph. What do you get?
en.concl: Rewrite eq. (1) as U = −Ir + E (textbook eq. 2): U-intercept = terminal voltage with an open circuit = E, slope magnitude = r; the crossing at U = 0 gives the short-circuit current, and r = E/I_sc is a second route that gives the same r.
points: U is on the vertical axis and I on the horizontal; the line has a negative slope.
U-intercept = terminal voltage with an open circuit = E; slope magnitude = r.
The crossing at U = 0 is the short-circuit current, and r = E/I_sc gives the same r.

en.q: With the y-axis starting at 0, what does the graph look like? Does the intercept change?
en.concl: Dry cells have small internal resistance and U changes little, so when plotting "the voltage axis generally doesn't start at 0" and the start should be chosen from the data (p.91); changing the axis range doesn't change the line, so p.90 asks "does the intercept change?". It doesn't (p.90 asks without answering; it follows from the equation), and the intercept is still E.
points: Dry cells have small internal resistance and U changes little, so the y-axis generally doesn't start at 0.
The start only changes the axis range; the line and intercept stay the same.
When the data are crowded together, say "adjust the axis range", not "the data are bad".

en.q: Record only the first two sets and solve the two points simultaneously. How far off is it?
en.concl: Solving two points simultaneously is mathematically fine, but readings go only to 0.01 and the two sets differ by just 0.03 A in I, so ΔU is only 2 in the last digit and dividing magnifies the error; that's why the textbook requires repeated measurements. The wider the span of the points, the closer the two-point method gets to the five-point method.
points: The two-point method is mathematically correct, but readings only go to 0.01 and ΔU is just 2 in the last digit.
The first two sets differ by only 0.03 A → r drifts to 0.67 Ω (+0.06 Ω).
Taking the first and last sets (I differs by 0.51 A) → back to 0.61 Ω: span is what matters.

en.q: Put the ammeter in the source branch and the voltmeter across the rheostat only. Is the measured r the same?
en.concl: With the circuit changed, E still measures 1.50 V, but r rises from 0.59 / 0.61 to 0.69 Ω (+0.09 Ω, +15 %, 9 in the last digit): the voltmeter misses the drop I·R_A across the ammeter, and that missing voltage all goes into the slope, so r comes out high by exactly the ammeter's internal resistance (not discussed in this textbook section; an L3 analytical derivation).
points: The circuit decides the direction of systematic error; it's not "just different readings".
Comparison circuit: E unbiased, r high by +R_A (+0.09 Ω at reading level, 9 in the last digit, visible as soon as you measure).
In this setting the main reading is the voltage across the rheostat, not the terminal voltage; the reading's name has to change with it.

en.q: Does the textbook circuit measure E and r high or low? Why can't you see it in the readings?
en.concl: With the textbook circuit, E_meas and r_meas are both low by the same proportion; the bias is 33 / 83 times smaller than the last digit of a 0.01 reading and simply invisible in 2-decimal readings, so the textbook text doesn't discuss it and spends its effort on repeated measurement, plotting and the y-axis start. The direction can only be calculated, not seen in readings (analytical derivation, not discussed in this textbook section, L3).
points: Meters aren't ideal: R_V draws current and R_A drops voltage (p.76 gives about 3 kΩ / 0.1 Ω).
With the textbook circuit, E_meas and r_meas are both low by the same 0.0200 % (k = R_V/(R_V+r)).
This bias is 33 / 83 times smaller than the last digit of the readings, so you can't see it; the direction can only be calculated.

en.q: Will E and r measured with the circuit on the bench pass?
en.concl: The test looks only at results: 5 sets under the same setup, E_meas within 0.01 V of 1.50 V, r_meas within 0.02 Ω of 0.60 Ω. The circuit itself isn't a criterion, but it decides the result: the comparison circuit adds the ammeter's internal resistance to r (0.69 Ω), while the textbook circuit's bias is only 0.0200 % and invisible in the readings.
points: Only three criteria: 5 sets under the same setup, E_meas within 0.01 V of 1.50 V, r_meas within 0.02 Ω of 0.60 Ω.
You start on the comparison circuit: 5 sets with it give 0.69 Ω, off by 0.09 → you have to think of switching back to the textbook circuit yourself.
Fewer than 5 sets won't pass either: the number of sets is part of "measuring".
